options.summary: A single, self-contained Command Line Interface (CLI) tool that orchestrates the entire process in-memory. It will parse Markdown files, compute backlinks, generate a search index, and render the final static HTML site in a single execution.

components.name: CLI Application
responsibilities: Handles user input (source/destination folders), orchestrates internal modules, and provides user feedback.

components.name: Content Processor
responsibilities: Reads Markdown files from the source directory.
Parses content, extracts frontmatter, tags, and link information.

components.name: Graph & Index Engine
responsibilities: Builds a graph of all notes from parsed link information to compute backlinks.
Generates a client-side full-text search index from note content.

components.name: Site Renderer
responsibilities: Converts processed content into final HTML pages using internal templates.
Assembles the output directory with all generated HTML, CSS, client-side JS, and the search index.

interfaces.contract: In-memory data structure containing all parsed notes, their metadata, and forward links.
In-memory data structure enriched with backlink information and the generated search index data.

pros: Simple user experience with a single command to run.
Potentially high performance due to in-memory processing, avoiding I/O overhead between stages.
Easier dependency management as it's a single, cohesive application.
cons: Monolithic design can be harder to maintain and extend over time.
Less flexibility to swap out individual parts like the Markdown parser or search library without code changes.
All logic is tightly coupled within one codebase.

risks: The monolithic codebase could become complex and difficult to refactor as new features are added.
Performance may suffer at very large scale (e.g., >10,000 notes) if in-memory data structures become too large, leading to high memory consumption.

options.summary: Leverage an existing extensible Static Site Generator (SSG) such as Eleventy. Core functionality like Markdown-to-HTML conversion and templating is handled by the SSG, while custom features like backlink generation and search indexing are implemented as plugins.

components.name: Core SSG Engine (e.g., Eleventy)
responsibilities: Provides the main build pipeline, including file watching, data loading, templating, and page generation.
Provides a plugin API to extend its functionality.

components.name: Data Preprocessor & Backlink Plugin
responsibilities: Hooks into the SSG's build process to read all content.
Builds a link graph across all notes and computes backlinks.
Exposes the backlink data globally to the SSG's templating engine.

components.name: Search Indexer Plugin
responsibilities: Generates a client-side search index file (e.g., JSON) during the SSG build process.
Places the generated index into the final site output directory.

components.name: Frontend Search Module
responsibilities: Client-side JavaScript that runs in the browser.
Fetches the search index file and initializes a search library.
Implements the search UI and displays results.

interfaces.contract: Global data object provided via SSG plugin API, making note graph and backlink information accessible within templates.
A static JSON search index file, generated during the build and fetched via an HTTP request by the client-side JavaScript in the browser.

pros: Significantly reduces development time by building on a mature, well-documented platform.
Gains access to a large ecosystem of existing themes and plugins.
Handles many common SSG problems out-of-the-box (e.g., live reload, asset pipelines).
cons: Constrained by the architecture, limitations, and performance of the chosen SSG.
Requires learning the specific plugin and data model of the SSG, which can have its own complexity.
Adds a dependency on a large, external open-source project and its release cycle.

risks: The chosen SSG may not provide the necessary hooks or flexibility to implement a specific feature, requiring complex workarounds.
Future updates to the core SSG could introduce breaking changes in the plugin APIs, requiring maintenance work.

options.summary: A pipeline of distinct, single-responsibility CLI tools that communicate via intermediate files in a standard data format (e.g., JSON). Each step (parsing, backlink analysis, indexing, rendering) is a separate, replaceable tool.

components.name: Content Parser
responsibilities: Scans a directory of Markdown files.
Outputs a single structured JSON file containing the content, metadata, and extracted forward links for every note.

components.name: Data Enricher
responsibilities: Consumes the structured JSON from the Content Parser.
Analyzes the link graph to compute backlinks for each note.
Outputs an enriched version of the JSON with this new data.

components.name: Search Indexer
responsibilities: Consumes the structured JSON from the Content Parser.
Generates a static client-side search index file.

components.name: Site Renderer
responsibilities: Consumes the enriched JSON from the Data Enricher.
Applies templates to generate final HTML pages.
Copies the generated pages, search index, and other static assets to the output directory.

interfaces.contract: Primary structured data file (e.g., notes.json) on disk containing parsed content and forward links.
Primary structured data file (e.g., notes.json) on disk containing parsed content and forward links.
Enriched data file (e.g., enriched-notes.json) on disk containing backlink information.
Generated search index file (e.g., search-index.json) on disk.

pros: Extremely flexible and modular; each component can be developed, tested, and replaced independently.
Components are simple, single-purpose, and easier to reason about.
Allows for mixing technologies (e.g., a parser in Rust, a renderer in Node.js).
cons: More complex build orchestration is required (e.g., using a Makefile or shell script).
Performance can be lower due to the I/O overhead of writing and reading intermediate files between each step.
Maintaining the consistency of the intermediate JSON format across tools can be challenging.

risks: The complexity of managing the multi-step build process could be a burden for the end-user compared to a single command.
Changes to the intermediate JSON schema require careful coordination and updates across multiple independent tools.
